claim: Secondary stress in English loans is contrastive in the loan stratum and systematically avoids vowels that are epenthetic relative to the English source.

source_forms.sample: about 500 recorded loans; 134 used for secondary-stress analysis
source_forms.cue: secondary stress identified primarily by local pitch rise/fall

formal_environment: loanword prosodic word; first two candidate secondary-stress vowels
normalized_environment: secondary stress disfavored on V with no English correspondent
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Not every token had a discernible secondary stress and such tokens were excluded; the effect is probabilistic, not categorical.

claim: When V2 corresponds to stressed English material, epenthetic V1 received secondary stress only 26% of the time versus 66% for a non-epenthetic V1 corresponding to an unstressed English vowel; conversely V1 stress was more frequent when V2 was epenthetic.
normalized_environment: stress choice conditioned by source-correspondence/epenthesis status
scope: qualifying loan tokens in reported table; three speakers
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Table cells are unbalanced and some combinations absent; authors therefore supplement raw comparisons with regression.

claim: Vowel deletion in loans is sensitive to whether the vowel is epenthetic relative to the English source: epenthetic vowels are significantly more likely to delete.

source_forms.model_result: epenthetic status coefficient 1.492, p=0.005 in reported model

formal_environment: loan vowel corresponding to English zero versus English vowel
normalized_environment: P(delete V) higher when V lacks English correspondent
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Deletion is variable and speaker-conditioned; source status changes probability rather than imposing deterministic deletion.

claim: Final vowel length in loans is conditioned by the status of the penultimate vowel: lengthening is most favored when the penult is epenthetic, less favored when it corresponds to an unstressed English vowel, and disfavored when it corresponds to a stressed English vowel.

source_forms.ordering: epenthetic penult > English-unstressed correspondent > English-stressed correspondent in probability of final-V length

normalized_environment: P(final V:) conditioned by penult source-correspondence and English stress
scope: loans whose final Tongan vowel corresponds to an unstressed English vowel
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Schütz's earlier observation was explicitly non-regular; the 2019 corpus demonstrates a probabilistic three-way effect rather than a categorical rule.

claim: The loan system preserves distributional distinctions absent from native Tongan: native phonology lacks lexical stress contrast and, for most consonant combinations, lacks a CC-versus-CVC contrast, while loans show marginal contrasts indirectly through secondary stress, deletion probabilities, and final-vowel length.

native_baseline: no general CC vs CVC contrast for most CC

normalized_environment: loan-specific marginal contrasts track English source structure without requiring novel surface segment types
scope: comparison drawn by authors from three case studies
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Effects are often gradient or indirect rather than clean minimal-pair contrasts; record should not be read as loans freely permitting native-illegal clusters.
